## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.55335.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.55335.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This paper combines an elegant cognitive task with sophisticated brain imaging approaches (functional MRI pattern analysis) to characterize the neural mechanisms that support memory retrieval in healthy older adults. While it is well known that memory declines with aging, our understanding of how neural variability – both across individuals and within an individual, on a moment-to-moment basis – might explain memory success or failure remains limited. Armed with a large sample size well-suited to address just these sorts of questions, the present study provides clear empirical evidence for unique hippocampal and cortical contributions to remembering in healthy older adults.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Hippocampal and cortical mechanisms at retrieval explain variability in episodic remembering in older adults" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Laura Colgin as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Lars Nyberg (Reviewer #2); Josh Koen (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

In this interesting and well-written study, the authors used functional magnetic resonance imaging to ask whether hippocampal pattern completion can account for some of the marked heterogeneity in episodic memory decline in healthy aging. Pattern completion was indexed with multivariate measures of cortical reinstatement (category- and event-level) and univariate hippocampal activity. Importantly, trial-by-trial measures of pattern completion in the ANG and VTC we related to successful associative memory retrieval and also account for some of the age-related declines in memory performance. Reviewers appreciated the sizeable sample of older adult participants, and highlighted the consideration of within-participant, trial-by-trial neural effects was a notable methodological advance. This paper will be an important contribution to the field for these reasons.

Essential revisions:

While reviewers are overall enthusiastic about this paper, there are a number of concerns identified that must be adequately addressed in a revision.

1) The reporting of the linear mixed effects models needs to be clearer in the paper. It was quite challenging to keep track of what predictors were included in each model when they were reported in the text. For example, please clarify what the "relevant nuisance variables" are and why they were deemed "relevant" for each model. One way to help this is to predictors in each model and their associated model coefficients in supplementary materials (including the random effects components). This has the added benefits of providing more information to readers to better evaluate the results. The reviewers acknowledge that this may be redundant with information on the GitHub repository (which was appreciated!), but note that not all readers will access that resource.

2) Reviewers were confused by reporting what are essentially the same models twice, with one set having age moderate the effect. This is particularly problematic as some of the effects in the first part of the results are actually moderated by age (for example, there was an Age Reinstatement interaction predicting AH success). Significant interactions with age make the earlier results from models that did not have an age interaction term more difficult to interpret. Reviewers request that the authors consider including only the larger models with the age-by-predictor of interest terms in the main paper, reporting whether the age-by-fixed effect interaction terms were significant or not. Additional models might be better put into the supplementary material if the authors deem them necessary to report. Reviewers believe this will improve the overall clarify of the statistical approach.

3) There are many known issues with interpreting mediation from cross-sectional samples (see Raz and Lindenburger, 2011, Psychological Bulletin; Maxwell and Cole, 2007, Psychological Methods), and thus the conclusions one can draw from them here are limited. Here, we note that the mediation analyses were not critical to the paper's main conclusions. As such, the reviewers recommend removing the mediation analyses to improve the flow of the paper and reduce the already large number of analyses. However, we acknowledge that this issue might still be debated in the field and that mediation analyses are regularly reported in cross-sectional studies. For this reason, reviewers believe it is the authors' right to decide the best course of action for their paper. If the authors elect to keep the mediation analysis, please add more details about it to the Materials and methods and discuss its limitations in a cross-sectional study.

4) There is growing appreciate in the literature about how fidelity of representation at encoding might explain some of the observed age differences in retrieval (at the behavioral or neural levels; for recent reviews, see Koen and Rugg, 2019, TICs; Koen et al., 2020, Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences). As such, it would be appropriate to include more about the simple relationships between encoding strength and the various retrieval measures. The authors state that encoding strength is correlated with reinstatement strength and subsequently include it as a covariate of no interest in their statistical models. I understand that this demonstrates that action at retrieval is an additional and important contributor. However, it seems as though more information on encoding strength on its own is warranted. Please report whether there are age effects on the encoding classification data. As I understand it, encoding strength does not "explain away" the age effects observed here – is that correct? At the conceptual level, I believe the relationship among hippocampal activity, reinstatement, and memory success should be intact even when encoding strength is weak, but perhaps this has a larger effect on the reinstatement piece (i.e., less on hippocampal activity)? While we understand the encoding classification data is not central to the aims of this paper, it deserves some mention to show that this task can replicate prior findings showing reductions in multivariate measures of neural selectivity (see Carp et al., 2011; Park et al., 2010; 2012; Koen et al., 2019). These papers also warrant citing in the relevant spots when discussing neural dedifferentiation.

5) As a methodological point (somewhat related to the possibility of dedifferentiation), how might encoding strength influence reinstatement at the level of activation patterns and correlations? In other words, if there is additional noise in the patterns at encoding, one might expect that to show up in subsequent analyses that also depend on these patterns (this would be true both for a classifier trained on the encoding data or the ERS analysis). This seems worth consideration in the paper, even if the authors do not believe it to be a relevant issue.

6) It is stated (Introduction) that aging may affect HPC, cortical reinstatement, and/or the brain-behavior link. While reviewers agree in principle, in view of the canonical model outlined in the 1st paragraph of the Introduction (cue => HC activation => cortical replay), it is unclear whether intact cortical reinstatement in principle could occur in the presence of dysfunctional HPC. The authors may want to elaborate on this. It is unclear whether the regression findings reported in the subsection “Unique Hippocampal and Cortical Contributions to Associative Retrieval” offer conclusive support that VTC and ANG can support successful associative retrieval independently of hippocampal activity (i.e. that they would be predictive in the absence of HC activity). This topic is also critical for the conclusion that age particularly affected the translation of cortical evidence to memory behavior (subsection “Effects of Age on Hippocampal and Cortical Indices of Pattern Completion”). The finding that HPC may be preserved but cortical reinstatement impaired in ageing is quite surprising in view of findings of preserved retrieval of detail semantic memories in older age, along with impairment on hippocampus-based episodic memory tasks. Please address this, perhaps in the Discussion.

7) Given the ideas that hippocampal activity should drive cortical reinstatement, one might expect the authors would test whether reinstatement (perhaps separately in VTC and ANG) mediates the relationship between hippocampal activity and associative memory success. Instead, the authors asked whether both explained some variance in performance when included in the same model. This seems to make a slightly different statistical point. It would be helpful for the authors to include some rationale for their decision of statistical test in light of the mechanism.

8) The analyses of cortical reinstatement focused on VTC and ANG, with the motivation that these areas support content-rich representations during retrieval and that their representations may be related to memory-guided behaviour. The VTC prediction was easy to follow, given face/place selectivity in this area. However, reviewers wanted more information on the role of ANG as an a priori region of interest. What type of processing is this region thought to perform? For example, would ANG involvement be expected if auditory information is studied rather than visual objects? That is, is this a region related to stimulus specificity or more generally related to successful retrieval ("memory guided behaviour")? If the latter, is it really to be expected to see "reactivation"/reinstatement of encoding activity in this region?

9) More justification is needed for grouping AM, IH, and IM into a single unsuccessful bin logistic mixed effects regression model. Doing so makes it difficult to know if the models are predicting associative memory success or simply item memory success. The more appropriate comparison might be to drop IM trials from this bin such that the AH vs. AM + IH controls for successful item memory. It would be important for the authors to somehow demonstrate that the results do not hinge on item miss trials being included in the "unsuccessful" bin. This analysis could be reported in the supplementary material. Also, it would be helpful to report the proportions of trials in each bin in supplementary material for readers to appreciate the relative mixture of trial types.

10) Some of the effects appear to depend on image category (according to Supplementary file 1E). This seems rather important to touch on in the main text. There is some inconsistency in the literature concerning if age-related neural dedifferentiation is ubiquitous or not across different visual stimuli (Voss et al., 2008; Koen et al., 2019; Payer et al., 2006; reviewed in Koen and Rugg, 2019; Koen et al., 2020). Thus, these category moderations deserve some mention in the main text. Please also address whether there are behavioral (memory) differences between faces and places, since substantial differences in performance across these trial types could influence the classification, as memory success/failure is confounded with face/place.

11) Please clarify how the fMRI measures were summarized for the individual difference analyses. Were they simply averaged across all trials, AH trials, or some other mixture? Also, why were age interactions excluded from the model? While the models suggest that the effects are independent of age, they do not imply that they are age invariant (Rugg, 2015). I appreciate that there might not be enough variability in this sample (which is only older adults) but demonstrating age invariance here seems important given the conclusions that are drawn.

12) The degree of variability in any given sample/study will in part be driven by the recruitment procedure. It is our impression that this sample was very healthy and cognitively intact (see Table 1) – and there was no relation between level of education and memory performance! This is at odds with findings in many published longitudinal studies. Comments on the sample in relation to the topic of heterogeneity would be informative.

13) Effects now attributed to influences of ageing in this cross-sectional study could be driven by other factors, and strong conclusions on the effects go ageing will have to await longitudinal follow-up studies. Please address this limitation in the paper.

1) Please clarify throughout the paper, figures (i.e., axis labels), and legends when the term "reinstatement strength" refers to category-level versus event-level reinstatement.

2) Please clarify what is meant by "univariate activity" in Supplementary file 1C. Are all univariate measures derived from hippocampus, or was activity from other ROIs (VTC, ANG) also included in some models as a control? Furthermore, what is the reason for sometimes using category-selective voxels and other times using whole-ROI activity? These details could be noted in the paper or table caption.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analyses presented in the results showing that cortical reinstatement partially mediates the effect of hippocampal activity on retrieval success.

claims.claim: Older age weakened cortical reinstatement and its relationship to memory behaviour.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analyses showing age-related decline in reinstatement strength and moderation effects of age on the relationship between reinstatement and behavior.

claims.claim: Episodic memory, particularly the ability to form and retrieve associations between multiple event elements, declines with age.
claims.source: Episodic memory – in particular the ability to form and retrieve associations between multiple event elements that comprise past experiences – declines with age (Spencer and Raz, 1995; Rönnlund et al., 2005; Old and Naveh-Benjamin, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on age-related memory decline.

claims.claim: Retrieval of an episodic memory relies critically on hippocampal-dependent pattern completion.
claims.source: Retrieval of an episodic memory relies critically on hippocampal-dependent pattern completion, which entails reactivation of a stored memory trace by the hippocampus in response to a partial cue, leading to replay of cortical activity patterns that were present at the time of memory encoding (Marr, 1971; McClelland et al., 1995; Tanaka et al., 2014; Staresina et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical models and empirical evidence cited in the introduction.

claims.claim: Pattern completion entails reactivation of a stored memory trace by the hippocampus in response to a partial cue, leading to replay of cortical activity patterns that were present at the time of memory encoding.

claims.evidence: This claim describes the theoretical mechanism of pattern completion and is supported by citations to computational and empirical work.

claims.claim: In vivo measures of pattern completion are linked to episodic remembering.
claims.source: Given observed links between in vivo measures of pattern completion and episodic remembering (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 2014), and evidence of altered hippocampal function with age (Lister and Barnes, 2009; Leal and Yassa, 2013), changes in hippocampal pattern completion may play an important role in explaining age-related impairments in episodic memory.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior empirical studies linking pattern completion measures to memory.

claims.claim: Hippocampal function is altered with age.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on age-related changes in hippocampal function.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies in younger adults.

claims.claim: Multivariate pattern analyses reveal evidence for cortical reinstatement of categorical event features during successful recollection.

claims.source: In each encoding block, participants viewed 24 word-picture pairs (12 word-face and 12 word-place) and were asked to intentionally form an association between each word and picture pair.

claims.claim: In each retrieval block, 24 target words were interspersed with 6 novel (foil) words; participants made a 4-way memory decision for each word.
claims.source: Following each encoding block, participants performed a retrieval task that probed item recognition and associative recollection. In each block, 24 target words were interspersed with 6 novel (foil) words; participants made a 4-way memory decision for each word.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the retrieval task.

claims.claim: After the MR scan session, a final overt cued-recall test was conducted outside the scanner to evaluate the degree to which participants were able to recollect the specific face or place associated with each target word.
claims.source: After the MR scan session, a final overt cued-recall test was conducted outside the scanner to evaluate the degree to which participants were able to recollect the specific face or place associated with each target word.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the post-scan memory test.

claims.claim: Data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner using a 32-channel radiofrequency receive-only head coil.
claims.source: Data were acquired on a 3T GE Discovery MR750 MRI scanner (GE Healthcare) using a 32-channel radiofrequency receive-only head coil (Nova Medical).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the MRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: Functional data were acquired using a multiband EPI sequence (acceleration factor = 3) consisting of 63 oblique axial slices parallel to the long axis of the hippocampus.
claims.source: Functional data were acquired using a multiband EPI sequence (acceleration factor = 3) consisting of 63 oblique axial slices parallel to the long axis of the hippocampus (TR = 2 s, TE = 30 ms, FoV = 215 mm x 215 mm, flip angle = 74, voxel size = 1.8 × 1.8 × 2 mm).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claims.claim: The hippocampal mask was defined manually using each participant's high-resolution T2-weighted structural image.
claims.source: The hippocampal mask was defined manually using each participant's high-resolution T2-weighted structural image using established procedures (Olsen et al., 2009), and comprised the whole hippocampus (see Figure 4—figure supplements 5–6 for analysis of hippocampal subfields).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the ROI definition procedures.

claims.claim: The VTC mask was composed of three anatomical regions: parahippocampal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal cortex.
claims.source: The VTC mask was composed of three anatomical regions: parahippocampal cortex, fusiform gyrus, and inferior temporal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the VTC ROI definition.

claims.claim: The ANG ROI was defined by the intersection of the Freesurfer inferior parietal lobe label and the Default Network of the Yeo 7 network atlas.
claims.source: The ANG ROI was defined by the intersection of the Freesurfer inferior parietal lobe label and the Default Network of the Yeo 7 network atlas (Yeo et al., 2011), defined on the Freesurfer average (fsaverage) cortical surface mesh.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the ANG ROI definition.

claims.claim: Classification was implemented using L2-penalized logistic regression models.
claims.source: Classification was implemented using Scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011), nilearn (Abraham et al., 2014), nibabel (Brett et al., 2016), and in house Python scripts, and performed using L2-penalized logistic regression models as instantiated in the LIBLINEAR classification library (regularization parameter C = 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the classification analysis methods.

claims.claim: A feature selection step was conducted, in which a subject-specific univariate contrast was used to identify the top 250 voxels that were most sensitive to each category during encoding, yielding a set of 500 voxels over which classification analyses were performed.
claims.source: A feature selection step was also conducted, in which a subject-specific univariate contrast was used to identify the top 250 voxels that were most sensitive to each category (face, place) during encoding, yielding a set of 500 voxels over which classification analyses were performed.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the feature selection procedure for classification analysis.

claims.claim: To measure category-level cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval, a classifier was trained on all encoding phase data, and then tested on all retrieval phase data.
claims.source: To measure category-level cortical reinstatement during memory retrieval, we trained a new classifier on all encoding phase data, and then tested on all retrieval phase data.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the classification analysis approach for measuring reinstatement.

claims.claim: The significance of classifier performance for each condition and ROI was assessed using permutation testing.
claims.source: The significance of classifier performance for each condition and ROI was assessed using permutation testing. We generated a null distribution for each participant by shuffling the trial labels over 1000 iterations for each of the 10 subsampling iterations, calculating mean classifier accuracy for each iteration.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the statistical approach for assessing classifier significance.

claims.claim: Pattern similarity analyses were used to measure event-level cortical reinstatement by computing the similarity (Pearson correlation) between trial-wise activity patterns extracted from ROIs during encoding and retrieval.
claims.source: To complement the classification analyses, we used pattern similarity analyses to measure event-level cortical reinstatement. This approach involved computing the similarity (Pearson correlation) between trial-wise activity patterns extracted from ROIs during encoding and retrieval (i.e., encoding-retrieval similarity; ERS).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the pattern similarity analysis approach.

claims.claim: Trial-wise analyses were conducted using mixed effects models (linear and logistic).
claims.source: All statistical analyses were implemented in the R environment (version 3.4.4). Trial-wise analyses were conducted using mixed effects models (linear and logistic) using the lmer4 statistical package (Bates et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach for trial-wise data.

claims.claim: Individual-differences analyses were conducted using multiple linear regression.
claims.source: Individual-differences analyses were conducted using multiple linear regression.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis approach for individual differences data.

results.result: Memory performance (old/new d', associative d', and post-scan exemplar-specific recall) declined with age but showed considerable individual variability. Performance did not vary by sex or education, and associative d' was higher for word-face than word-place pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 report significant age-related declines in all three memory measures with appropriate statistical tests (β values and p-values). Claims C40-C41 show no effects of sex or education. Claim C42 demonstrates a stimulus category effect. Claim C43 notes individual variability, which is evident in the figures. All claims are supported by appropriate statistical analyses and visualizations.

results.result: In-scanner associative memory performance strongly predicted post-scan exemplar-specific recall at both the individual and trial-wise levels, suggesting that post-scan recall approximates in-scanner memory for specific exemplars.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45 provide strong statistical evidence (β = 0.62, p < 10^-12 for individual differences; χ²(1) = 159.68, p < 10^-36 for trial-wise) linking in-scanner and post-scan performance. Claim C46 is a reasonable inference from these strong correlations, though the authors appropriately acknowledge quantitative differences due to retention interval and interference.

results.result: Encoding classifiers successfully discriminated face and place categories in both VTC and ANG, with above-chance accuracy in all participants. Classifier accuracy was higher in VTC than ANG and did not vary with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 report classifier accuracies well above chance (VTC: 98.4%, ANG: 90.0%) with appropriate statistical tests and permutation testing. Claim C49 shows a significant difference between regions. Claim C51 shows no age effect. These are methodological validation results that are well-supported by the data.

results.result: Encoding classifier strength predicted category-level reinstatement strength during retrieval at both trial-wise and individual difference levels in both VTC and ANG.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 report significant relationships between encoding and retrieval classifier strength with appropriate statistical tests (trial-wise: VTC χ²(1) = 13.96, p < 0.001; ANG χ²(1) = 30.16, p < 10^-8; individual differences: VTC β = 0.45, p < 10^-5; ANG β = 0.62, p < 10^-11). The authors appropriately control for this relationship in subsequent analyses.

results.result: Category-level cortical reinstatement was above chance during associative hits but not during unsuccessful retrieval in both VTC and ANG. Reinstatement was stronger in ANG than VTC, stronger for places than faces in VTC, and emerged 4-6 seconds post-stimulus onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 report classifier accuracies with appropriate permutation testing showing above-chance performance only during successful retrieval. Claims C59-C61 report regional and stimulus category differences with appropriate statistical tests. Claim C62 describes the time course with reference to supplementary figures. All claims are well-supported by the classification analyses.

results.result: Trial-wise category-level cortical reinstatement strength in VTC and ANG was positively related to the probability of associative hits, post-scan exemplar-specific recall, and faster reaction times on associative hit trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 report significant relationships between reinstatement strength and multiple behavioral measures using appropriate mixed effects models with highly significant p-values (all p < 10^-6 for accuracy measures, p < 10^-6 for RT). The trial-wise approach and statistical methods are appropriate for the data structure.

results.result: Age moderated the relationship between VTC category-level reinstatement strength and memory behavior, with older individuals showing weaker relationships between reinstatement and both associative retrieval success and reaction time. This effect was marginally significant in ANG for retrieval success.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 report age moderation effects with appropriate statistical tests (VTC: χ²(1) = 7.12, p < 0.01 for accuracy; χ²(1) = 3.91, p < 0.05 for RT; ANG: χ²(1) = 3.57, p = 0.059 for accuracy). Claim C73 is a reasonable inference from these moderation effects, though the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Event-level reinstatement was present during associative hits in both VTC and ANG. Trial-wise event-level reinstatement strength was related to increased probability of associative hits (in ANG) and post-scan exemplar-specific recall (in both regions), but not to reaction time. These relationships were not moderated by age.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 report significant event-level reinstatement with appropriate statistical tests. Claims C76-C80 report relationships with behavioral measures, with some effects reaching significance (ANG for associative hits, both regions for post-scan recall) and others not (VTC for associative hits, both regions for RT). Claim C81 reports no age moderation. The pattern of results is clearly reported with appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Hippocampal activity showed a graded response across memory conditions, with greatest activity during associative hits, intermediate activity during associative misses and item hits, and lowest activity during item misses and correct rejections.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 report a clear pattern of hippocampal activity across memory conditions with appropriate statistical comparisons (all p < 0.001 for significant differences). The graded pattern is consistent with theoretical predictions about hippocampal pattern completion and is well-supported by the univariate fMRI analyses.

results.result: Trial-wise hippocampal activity was positively related to the probability of associative hits and post-scan exemplar-specific recall, but not to reaction time. These relationships were not moderated by age and were strongest in the DG/CA3 subfield.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 report relationships between hippocampal activity and behavioral measures with appropriate mixed effects models (χ²(1) = 63.45, p < 10^-15 for associative hits; χ²(1) = 59.02, p < 10^-14 for post-scan recall; no significant effect for RT). Claim C93 reports no age moderation. Claim C94 reports subfield specificity with reference to supplementary figures. All claims are well-supported.

results.result: Trial-wise hippocampal activity significantly varied with category-level cortical reinstatement strength in both VTC and ANG across all retrieval attempts and when restricted to associative hits. Hippocampal activity also varied with event-level reinstatement in VTC but not ANG. These relationships were not moderated by age.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 report significant relationships between hippocampal activity and category-level reinstatement with appropriate statistical tests (all p < 0.05). Claims C99-C101 report relationships with event-level reinstatement, with significant effects in VTC but not ANG. Claim C102 reports no age moderation. The pattern of results supports the hypothesis that hippocampal activity relates to cortical reinstatement.

results.result: Hippocampal activity, VTC reinstatement, and ANG reinstatement each explained unique variance in associative retrieval success when included in the same model, with all three remaining significant predictors. This indicates that these measures, though related, provide complementary information about pattern completion.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 report nested model comparisons showing that each neural measure improves model fit and remains significant in the full model (all p < 10^-16). Claims C106-C107 are reasonable inferences from these model comparison results. The statistical approach is appropriate for assessing unique contributions of correlated predictors.

results.result: Category-level cortical reinstatement in both VTC and ANG partially mediated the relationship between hippocampal activity and associative retrieval success.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 report significant indirect effects from mediation analyses with appropriate bootstrap confidence intervals (VTC: b = 0.026, 95% CI = 0.016, 0.036; ANG: b = 0.019, 95% CI = 0.006, 0.032). Claim C110 is a direct inference from these results. The mediation analysis is appropriate for testing the hypothesis that cortical reinstatement mediates hippocampal effects on memory.

results.result: Hippocampal activity did not vary with age, but category-level reinstatement strength declined with age in both VTC and ANG, and event-level reinstatement declined with age in VTC but not ANG. Neural measures did not vary with sex or education.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 report age effects on neural measures with appropriate regression analyses. The pattern shows differential age effects across measures (no effect for hippocampal activity, significant effects for category-level reinstatement in both regions, effect for event-level reinstatement only in VTC). Claim C116 reports no effects of sex or education. All claims are supported by appropriate statistical tests.

results.result: Individual differences in hippocampal activity and category-level reinstatement strength (but not event-level reinstatement) during associative hits explained significant variance in exemplar-specific recall, independent of age.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C119 report significant relationships between neural measures and memory performance with appropriate regression analyses controlling for age (all p < 0.001). Claim C120 reports no significant relationship for event-level reinstatement. Claim C121 is a reasonable inference from these results. The statistical approach is appropriate for assessing individual differences.

results.result: The relationships between neural measures (hippocampal activity and category-level reinstatement) and exemplar-specific recall were not significantly moderated by age, suggesting age-invariant relationships, though this should be interpreted with caution given the restricted age range.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 report no significant age moderation effects with appropriate statistical tests. Claim C124 is an inference from these results, but the authors appropriately note caution due to the restricted age range (60-82 years). The lack of moderation is clearly stated with appropriate caveats about interpretation.

results.result: Hierarchical regression showed that hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement explained unique variance in exemplar-specific recall beyond age, while VTC and ANG reinstatement explained shared variance. Together, these measures explained substantial variance in memory performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 report hierarchical regression results showing that each neural measure explains additional variance beyond age (all p < 0.01). Claim C128 shows that ANG reinstatement is no longer significant when VTC reinstatement is included. Claims C129-C130 are reasonable inferences from these model comparison results. The hierarchical regression approach is appropriate for assessing unique and shared contributions.

results.result: Hippocampal activity and VTC category-level reinstatement strength were significant predictors of delayed recall performance on standardized neuropsychological tests, and these measures explained unique variance in delayed recall.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 report significant relationships between neural measures and standardized test performance with appropriate regression analyses (both p < 0.01). Claim C133 reports no significant relationship for ANG reinstatement. Claim C134 shows that both measures explain unique variance. These results demonstrate that the neural measures predict memory performance across different assays.

results.result: Neural measures (hippocampal activity and VTC reinstatement) explained variance in exemplar-specific recall beyond that explained by standardized neuropsychological tests, indicating that task-based fMRI measures provide information not captured by traditional memory tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 report hierarchical regression results showing that neural measures remain significant predictors even after controlling for standardized test performance (both p < 10^-5). Claims C137-C138 are reasonable inferences from these results. The finding that neural measures explain unique variance beyond standardized tests is important for demonstrating the added value of fMRI measures.

results.result: The trial-wise relationships between hippocampal activity, cortical reinstatement, and memory behavior observed in older adults extend prior work in younger adults and are consistent with theoretical models of hippocampal pattern completion. These relationships did not vary with age and were strongest in DG/CA3.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 are inferences based on the trial-wise findings interpreted in the context of prior work and theoretical models. Claims C143-C144 report no age moderation of trial-wise relationships. While the inferences about mechanisms are speculative (as the authors acknowledge regarding directionality with fMRI), the empirical findings supporting these inferences are well-documented in the results.

results.result: The positive relationship between hippocampal activity during associative hits and memory performance was observed across hippocampal subfields and did not vary with age, consistent with proposals that hippocampal function is important for memory maintenance in older adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 are inferences based on the individual differences findings showing positive relationships between hippocampal activity and memory that do not vary with age. Claims C148-C149 interpret these findings in the context of prior theoretical proposals. The empirical findings are well-supported, though the theoretical interpretations are necessarily speculative.

results.result: Trial-wise reinstatement strength was tightly linked to memory behavior (accuracy and speed), suggesting graded rather than all-or-none retrieval. The category-level reinstatement effects likely reflect a combination of different retrieval outcomes, and the relationship between reinstatement and behavior may reflect reduced monitoring demands or greater confidence.
results.evaluation: Claim C152 is supported by the trial-wise findings showing relationships between reinstatement and both accuracy and RT. Claims C153-C159 are inferences and speculations about the nature of retrieval and the mechanisms underlying the observed relationships. While speculative, these interpretations are reasonable given the data and are appropriately presented as possibilities rather than definitive conclusions.

results.result: Age effects on reinstatement strength were observed after controlling for encoding classifier performance, indicating that variance in reinstatement strength reflects retrieval precision rather than simply encoding differentiation. This provides neuroimaging evidence for proposals that age-related memory decline involves loss of mnemonic precision.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 is supported by the statistical approach of controlling for encoding strength. Claims C161-C163 cite prior work on encoding differentiation and its relationship to reinstatement. Claims C164-C166 are inferences from the finding that reinstatement explains variance beyond encoding differentiation. The inference that reinstatement reflects retrieval precision is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: Hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement may index distinct aspects of recollection (retrieval success vs. retrieval precision), or cortical reinstatement may be differentially affected by top-down control and decision processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C167-C169 are speculative interpretations of why hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement explain unique variance in memory performance. While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations to prior theoretical work, they remain speculative and are not directly tested in the current study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities.

results.result: Variability in memory and pattern completion metrics is likely influenced by multiple factors beyond those measured in this study, including age-related changes in retrieval monitoring, encoding processes, and attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 acknowledge limitations of the study and cite prior work on other factors that may influence memory in aging. This is an appropriate acknowledgment of the complexity of memory processes and the limitations of the current study. The claims are supported by citations to relevant prior work.

results.result: Hippocampal and cortical indices of pattern completion play a central role in determining memory success, predicted relationships can be observed in older adults, and these neural metrics explain unique variance across individuals. The neural measures may represent sensitive biomarkers of hippocampal and cortical function.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C175 are inferences based on the trial-wise and individual differences findings. Claims C176-C177 are inferences about the stability and potential utility of the neural measures as biomarkers. While the inference about biomarker utility is somewhat speculative, the empirical findings supporting these inferences are well-documented.

results.result: Neural indices provide information beyond standardized tests, and combining neural metrics with existing tools can build more accurate models of memory performance. Future work should assess whether combining task-related neural measures with other biomarkers can further increase sensitivity for predicting memory decline.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C179 are inferences based on the finding that neural measures explain variance beyond standardized tests. Claim C180 is speculation about future research directions. The empirical basis for claims C178-C179 is well-supported, while C180 is appropriately presented as a future direction.

results.result: Hippocampal activity and cortical reinstatement provide a partial account for memory variability in older adults, predict individual differences across memory assays, and may be differentially affected by age. The high within-group variance likely contributes to mixed findings in the literature, and an individual differences approach can advance understanding of memory mechanisms in aging.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C182 are inferences based on the trial-wise and individual differences findings. Claim C183 is an inference about differential age effects with appropriate caution about the cross-sectional design. Claims C184-C185 are inferences about the implications of the findings for the literature and future research. All inferences are reasonable given the data.
